F-strings embed expressions inside text: f"Total: {price * 2:.2f}" formats a number with two decimals. Integer division // discards the fractional part (7 // 2 is 3), the modulo operator % returns the remainder (7 % 2 is 1), and ** is exponentiation (2 ** 10 is 1024). Dividing with / always returns a float, so 6 / 3 is 2.0.

S2.title: Python Reference Notes
S2.text:
COMMON ERRORS AND THEIR MEANING
SyntaxError: the code is not valid Python, for example a missing colon after if.
IndentationError: the indentation of a block is inconsistent.
NameError: a variable or function name was used before it was defined.
TypeError: an operation was applied to the wrong type, such as "a" + 1.
ValueError: the type is right but the value is not, such as int("abc").
KeyError: a dictionary key does not exist.
IndexError: a list index is outside the valid range.
ZeroDivisionError: division or modulo by zero.
FileNotFoundError: the file path does not exist.

S3.title: Data Wrangling Handbook
S3.text:
5. Three Kinds of Index
A database index is a data structure that speeds up lookups on a column but makes writes slower
and uses extra storage. A pandas Index holds the row labels of a DataFrame. A Python list index is
an integer position starting at 0. These three meanings of the word index are unrelated.

S4.title: Python Lecture Notes
S4.text: 1. Variables and Data Types A variable is a name that refers to a value stored in memory. In Python you create a variable by assignment, for example age = 21. Python is dynamically typed: the type belongs to the value, not to the name, so the same name can later refer to a string. The core built-in types are int (whole numbers), float (decimal numbers), str (text), bool (True or False) and NoneType (the single value None, meaning "no value"). The function type(x) reports the type of x. Conversion functions such as int("42"), float("3.5") and str(10) create new values of another type; int("abc") raises a ValueError. Strings are immutable sequences of characters. Indexing starts at zero, so "python"[0] is "p", and negative indexes count from the end, so "python"[-1] is "n". Slicing "python"[1:4] returns "yth" (start included, stop excluded).
